activities.caption: the descendants — pair each classical tool with its computational heir
activities.name: scDescMatch

config.prompt: Every classical mechanism gained a computational descendant — pair them:

pairs.right: the pseudorandom generator that replaced it
the simulation study — data with known truth, bias measured directly

pairs.left: the survey question, open or closed
pairs.right: a typed column in a dataframe, with all the precision and fragility that implies

pairs.left: a claim resting on a sampling or measurement choice
pairs.right: simulate the choice first, and only then trust it

config.why: Read the classical data-collection unit through the lens of code: the mechanics stayed, the machinery changed.

activities.anchor: what makes the whole thing checkable
activities.caption: one card summary is wrong — click it
activities.name: scCardsSpot

config.prompt: One summary of the four cards is wrong — click it:
lines: Fisher imagined shuffling labels in 1935; a laptop runs the same idea a million times over lunch.
The bootstrap is that brute force aimed at your own sample — resample it, and the spread of the results is the uncertainty.
A simulation study feeds a method fake data with known truth and checks whether it recovers that truth.
Fixed seeds make an analysis harder to reproduce, so serious scripts avoid them.
config.correction: A fixed seed does the opposite: same seed → same sample → same result, turning the analysis into a re-runnable object.
config.why: Scripts, environments and seeds are the infrastructure that lets anyone re-run your analysis — card four is a feature, not an obstacle.

activities.caption: call the standard error before the formula does
activities.name: scSeEst

config.prompt: A pollster samples n = 100 voters and reports a percentage near 50. Roughly what is the standard error, in percentage points?
config.why: √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 100) = 0.05 — five points either way, which is why a poll at 55% versus another at 63% is routine fluctuation, not news.
config.context: The width is fixed by n before anyone is sampled — and the cloud of a thousand sample means comes out approximately normal.

activities.anchor: converge precisely on the biased view
activities.caption: true or false — what sample size can and cannot buy
activities.name: scSizeJudge

statements.s: A bigger sample shrinks random error.
statements.why: Averages of many draws wobble less — that is the part of the error that n buys down.

statements.s: A bigger sample shrinks systematic error the same way.
statements.why: Bias rides on the selection mechanism, which n never touches.

statements.s: A census is automatically better than any sample.
statements.why: Nonresponse and hard-to-reach groups leave most real censuses behaving like enormous, expensive, slightly broken samples.

statements.s: Given a large poll with a skewed selection and a small poll with a representative selection, trust the large one.
statements.why: Representativeness, not size, is what a sample owes you.

activities.caption: four schemes on trial — file each by its selection
activities.name: scSampSort

config.prompt: Four selection schemes — which ones keep the randomness honest?

items.label: every member gets an equal chance — the default all theory assumes
every kth unit after a random start (850 pupils, k ≈ 8 or 9)
randomly within strata — inpatients around 6.2, outpatients 7.9, proportional allocation
20 men over 60, whatever the interviewer's convenience provides
every 7th house on a street whose list carries a weekly rhythm

config.why: The random start is what keeps systematic sampling a probability method; quota looks representative, but the choosing hand belongs to the interviewer.

activities.caption: you are the detector — walk the audit
activities.name: scDetBranch

config.root: You are the computational bias detector. Walk the audit of a poll.

start.text: The sample's age and regional mix disagrees with the census benchmark. What now?

choices.label: Compare against the known totals, then reweight
choices.feedback: Comparison against known totals plus reweighting — both trivial in code.

choices.label: Trust it — the poll is enormous
choices.feedback: Size reduces random error, not systematic error; a million respondents from a skewed frame stay skewed.

audited.text: The weights balance the mix. What question remains before you report?

choices.label: Was the sampling frame itself right?
choices.feedback: Both detectors are useless if the frame was wrong — no weight restores a household the frame never listed.

choices.label: Publish, with the audit trail
choices.feedback: Log every exclusion and report how many records each cleaning rule removed.

frame.text: Dead end — a wrong frame cannot be reweighted into truth. Write the cleaning rules before seeing outcomes, and the audit trail separates data curation from data corruption.

sizeTrap.text: Dead end — systematic error survives any n. The selection mechanism owns this bias, not the sample size.

publish.text: Reported: benchmark comparison, reweighting, logged exclusions. The analysis is a re-runnable object, not a memory.

config.why: The computational detectors are cheap; the sampling frame they run on is the bottleneck.

activities.caption: from table to Twister — rebuild the lineage
activities.name: scGenOrder

config.prompt: Random sampling, mechanised — order the lineage:
items: Number every member (pupils 001–850), read three-digit groups off a random number table, accept 001–850, skip 000 and 851–999 and repeats
Von Neumann's middle-square (1946): square the seed, keep the middle digits — fast, but it collapses to zero
The Mersenne Twister — today's default in R and Python, period 2^19937 − 1
Run the same script with the same seed: same sample, same bootstrap — the analysis becomes a re-runnable object
config.why: The recipe never changed — only the table became an algorithm, and its determinism became reproducibility.

config.q: You run the same sampling script twice with the same seed. What comes out the second time?
choices: Two different samples — that is what random means
The identical sample, draw for draw
The same summary statistics, but different individual draws
An error — seeds cannot be reused
config.why: Pseudorandom generators produce deterministic streams seeded with a number: same seed, same sample, every time. For sampling from a finite population that is fine — and it is exactly why a fixed seed belongs in every serious script.
